statement: A finite Markov decision process (Definition 1) consists of a finite state set S with terminal subset S bar, finite action set A, reward function R: S x A x S -> R, transition function T: S x A x S -> [0,1] with per-(s,a) normalization (Eq. 2.1), and initial-state distribution mu with per-terminal-state zero mass (Eq. 2.2).
conditions: finite state and action spaces as given by Definition 1; continuous-state/action MDPs are noted as analogously definable but not formally given here
limits: the reward function as defined is deterministic given (s,a,s'); a probabilistic-reward variant is noted separately, not part of Definition 1 itself

statement: The Markov property states that the probability of the next state and reward is conditionally independent of past states and actions given the current state and action: Pr(s_{t+1}, r_t | s_t, a_t, s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}, ..., s_0, a_0) = Pr(s_{t+1}, r_t | s_t, a_t) (Eq. 2.3).
conditions: assumes the fully observable, finite-state MDP model of this section
limits: none stated beyond the definitional scope of the MDP model

statement: Dynamic programming algorithms (policy iteration, value iteration) require complete knowledge of the MDP's reward function R and transition function T, whereas temporal-difference learning algorithms (Sarsa, Q-learning) learn optimal value functions and policies from sampled interaction experience without requiring this complete knowledge.
conditions: applies to the tabular, model-based-vs-model-free framing given in Chapter 2
limits: this scope statement is specific to Chapter 2's tabular treatment; function-approximation variants of DP/TD are deferred to Chapters 7-8, outside this reader's range

statement: The Bellman equation for V^pi in a finite MDP is a system of m = |S| linear equations with a unique solution, exactly solvable (e.g. via Gauss elimination) with time complexity O(m^3) when the full MDP is known; this exact-solution cost motivates the iterative approximation methods (e.g. iterative policy evaluation) used in practice for larger state spaces.
evidence_type: textbook exposition citing a standard complexity result
conditions: full knowledge of R and T required; policy pi fixed for the policy-evaluation linear system
limits: applies to exact tabular solution via Gauss elimination only; does not address the time complexity of the iterative methods themselves, sample complexity, or function approximation

statement: The Bellman operator for V^pi is shown to be a gamma-contraction under the max-norm (||f^pi(v) - f^pi(u)||_inf <= gamma ||v-u||_inf, derived in Eq. 2.29-2.37), so by the Banach fixed-point theorem repeated application of iterative policy evaluation converges to the unique fixed point V^pi.
conditions: finite MDP, discount factor gamma < 1 (contraction property), tabular value representation
limits: the contraction property of the Bellman operator is derived in-text; the Banach fixed-point theorem itself is cited as background, not proven

statement: In the worked Mars Rover MDP example, value iteration under discount factor gamma=0.95 converges to optimal state values V*(Start)=4.1, V*(Site A)=6.2, V*(Site B)=10 with an optimal policy choosing 'left' then 'right' at both sites, whereas under gamma=0.5 the optimal policy instead chooses 'right' at the initial state with V*(Start)=0 — the identical MDP yields different optimal policies for different discount factors.

statement: A normal-form game (Definition 2) consists of a finite agent set I = {1,...,n} and, for each agent i, a finite action set A_i and reward function R_i: A -> R where A = A_1 x ... x A_n; agents select policies independently and simultaneously, and each receives a reward based on the resulting joint action.
conditions: finite agent set and finite per-agent action sets
limits: no environment state is present in this model; a single interaction only (extended to repetition in Section 3.2)

statement: The book's game-model hierarchy (Figure 3.1) states that partially observable stochastic games (POSGs) include stochastic games as the special case of full observability, stochastic games include repeated normal-form games as the special case of a single environment state, and repeated normal-form games (and stochastic games) include Markov decision processes as the special case of a single agent.
conditions: applies to the finite-state/finite-action formulations given in this chapter
limits: continuous-state/action variants are noted elsewhere as analogously definable but are not part of this stated hierarchy figure

statement: A partially observable stochastic game (Definition 4) extends the stochastic game by defining, for each agent i, a finite observation set O_i and observation function O_i: A x S x O_i -> [0,1] (Eq. 3.4); agents condition their policy on their own observation history h_i^t rather than the true environment state.
conditions: the common special case presented has each agent's observation function depend on the joint action a_{t-1} and new state s_t (not the previous state s_{t-1})
limits: a fully general form Pr(s_t, o_t | s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}) is stated first; the per-agent O_i form is presented as the common special case used throughout the book, not the only possible formulation

statement: Communication actions can be added to a stochastic game or POSG's per-agent action space as A_i = X_i x M_i, and the book defines the transition function to be invariant to the communication component of the joint action (Eq. 3.7: T(s'|s,a) = T(s'|s, <(a^x_1,m_1),...,(a^x_n,m_n)>) for any m in M), so that communication actions are observable by other agents but do not affect environment-state transitions by construction.
conditions: applies whenever the action space is factored as A_i = X_i x M_i and the transition function is defined by the authors to ignore the M component, as a stipulated modeling convention
limits: this is a modeling choice/definition made by the authors, not a proven general property of all game models that include communication

statement: Under the standard MARL knowledge assumption the book adopts, agents typically know neither their own nor other agents' reward functions, nor the state-transition or observation functions, and instead learn from experienced (state, joint action, reward, observation) tuples; this contrasts with the 'complete knowledge game' assumption standard in classical game theory. The book notes exceptions exist for zero-sum or common-reward games, where the specific reward structure is exploited in algorithm design (pointing to Chapters 6 and 9).
evidence_type: textbook exposition (stated modeling convention for the book)
conditions: applies to the book's stated default MARL setting; the simulator abstraction T-hat (Eq. 3.8) is offered as an intermediate case some MARL settings use instead
limits: the stated exceptions (zero-sum/common-reward algorithm design exploiting reward structure) are pointed to in Chapters 6 and 9, outside this reader's range, and are not themselves detailed here

statement: The book states its standard assumption throughout is that the number of agents in a game is fixed and this fact is commonly known by all agents; it explicitly states that open multi-agent environments, where agents dynamically enter and leave, are outside the scope of the book, citing only external prior work.
conditions: n/a
limits: this book's own game models and algorithms, as presented, are not evidence for variable-N (open-roster) generalization; the cited works (Jiang et al. 2020; Rahman et al. 2021; Rahman, Carlucho, et al. 2023) are external and are not reproduced or evaluated in this book

statement: A minimax solution for a two-agent zero-sum game (Definition 5) requires that agent i's maxmin value equal its minmax value; every finite two-agent zero-sum normal-form game has a minimax solution (von Neumann 1928; von Neumann and Morgenstern 1944), and finite-horizon or discounted infinite-horizon two-agent zero-sum stochastic games also have minimax solutions (Shapley 1953); all minimax solutions in a game yield the same unique value to each agent.
conditions: two-agent zero-sum games; finite game models (finite state/action/observation spaces); for stochastic games, finite episode length or discounted infinite episodes
limits: existence proofs are not reproduced in this text, only cited; continuous-action zero-sum games can lack a minimax value (cited to Sion and Wolfe 1957, footnote)

statement: A Nash equilibrium (Definition 6) is a joint policy in which no agent i can improve its expected return by unilaterally deviating, holding all other agents' policies fixed (Eq. 4.16); Nash (1950) proved every finite general-sum normal-form game has at least one Nash equilibrium.
conditions: general-sum games with n>=2 agents; finite normal-form games for the cited existence result
limits: existence for stochastic games is a separate cited result (Fink 1964; Filar and Vrieze 2012), not proved in text; a Nash equilibrium's action probabilities can be irrational for 3+ agents (Nash 1950)

statement: An epsilon-Nash equilibrium (Definition 7, Eq. 4.18) relaxes strict Nash equilibrium to allow at most epsilon improvement from unilateral deviation, but the authors give an explicit counterexample (Figure 4.2) in which an epsilon-Nash equilibrium's expected returns can be arbitrarily far from any real Nash equilibrium's returns, even when the Nash equilibrium is unique.
conditions: general-sum games with n agents, epsilon > 0
limits: the counterexample shows epsilon-Nash should not be interpreted as a return-approximation of Nash equilibrium; this is a stated conceptual limitation, not a universal impossibility proof

statement: Correlated equilibrium (Definition 8, Eq. 4.19) generalizes Nash equilibrium by allowing agents' actions to be jointly correlated via a shared recommendation policy; the set of correlated equilibria contains the set of Nash equilibria, with Nash equilibrium being the special case where the joint recommendation policy factors into independent per-agent policies (Osborne and Rubinstein 1994).
conditions: general-sum normal-form games with n agents; the recommendation policy is commonly known and each agent observes only its own recommended action
limits: the containment result is cited (Osborne and Rubinstein 1994), not proved in this text

statement: In the Chicken matrix game, a correlated equilibrium exists that gives both agents an expected return of 5, exceeding the return (about 4.66 each) of the best symmetric Nash equilibrium reachable under independent policies, illustrating that allowing correlation can strictly improve on what independent (Nash) policies achieve.
conditions: non-repeated Chicken matrix game, specific correlated policy pi_c(L,L)=pi_c(S,L)=pi_c(L,S)=1/3, pi_c(S,S)=0
limits: single hand-worked matrix-game example; not a general separation theorem between correlated and Nash equilibrium values

statement: Welfare optimality (maximizing the sum of agents' expected returns, Eq. 4.26) implies Pareto optimality (proof given by contradiction, p. 109), but the converse does not hold; fairness optimality (maximizing the product of agents' expected returns, Eq. 4.27, i.e. Nash social welfare) neither implies nor is implied by Pareto optimality.
conditions: general-sum games; welfare and fairness defined per Definitions 10-11
limits: welfare and fairness as defined here add no discriminating power in common-reward games or two-agent zero-sum games (all Pareto-optimal / all minimax solutions tie); the simple fairness definition breaks down when any agent's return is zero or negative (footnote 15)

statement: No-regret (Definition 12, Eq. 4.28-4.29) requires an agent's average regret across episodes, relative to the best fixed action/policy against the other agents' observed play, to go to zero in the limit; the authors state this assumes the other agents' actions/policies remain fixed retrospectively, which does not hold when opponents also adapt, so regret does not represent a true counterfactual and minimizing regret need not maximize returns (illustrated via Prisoner's Dilemma, where the unique no-regret joint policy is mutual defection).
conditions: general-sum games with n agents, average regret defined over a finite policy space Pi_i per agent
limits: explicit conceptual limitation stated by the authors; regret-based analysis assumes fixed comparator opponent behavior within the episode window being analyzed

statement: In two-agent zero-sum normal-form games, the empirical distribution of joint actions produced by no-external-regret play converges to the set of minimax solutions; in general-sum normal-form games, no-external-regret play converges to the set of coarse correlated equilibria, and no-internal-regret play converges to the set of correlated equilibria (Hart and Mas-Colell 2000; Young 2004).
conditions: normal-form games; convergence is of the empirical (time-averaged) joint-action distribution, not the joint policy itself
limits: cited result, not proved in this text; result is about normal-form games, and convergence is in the weaker empirical-distribution sense (Eq. 5.7), not pointwise

statement: Computing an equilibrium satisfying an additional decision-problem property -- Pareto optimality, a minimum per-agent expected return, a minimum social welfare, or fixed action-support constraints -- is NP-hard (Gilboa and Zemel 1989; Conitzer and Sandholm 2008), whereas minimax solutions (via linear programming, Section 4.3.1) and correlated equilibria (via linear programming, Section 4.6.1) are both computable in polynomial time.
conditions: non-repeated normal-form games
limits: NP-hardness results are cited, not proved in this text

statement: Computing a Nash equilibrium (NASH) in general-sum non-repeated normal-form games is PPAD-complete: proven first for games with three or more agents (Daskalakis, Goldberg, and Papadimitriou 2006, 2009), then for exactly two agents (Chen and Deng 2006); the approximate epsilon-Nash version is PPAD-complete for certain bounds on epsilon, and the exact (epsilon=0) version is PPAD-complete for two-agent games.
conditions: general-sum non-repeated normal-form games
limits: the theorem is cited from the named papers, not proved in this text; PPAD-completeness does not itself prove no polynomial algorithm exists (P=PPAD? remains open), only that finding one would resolve a decades-open question

statement: The PPAD-completeness of NASH (Section 4.11.2) establishes that no known efficient (polynomial-time) algorithm computes Nash equilibria for general games without exploiting additional structure or assumptions; it does not by itself say anything about the computational difficulty of the narrower or differently-scoped objectives used by non-equilibrium-seeking MARL methods, such as objectives built around skill discovery, intrinsic reward, or common-reward maximization rather than Nash-equilibrium computation.
conditions: applies specifically to the stated problem of computing (epsilon-)Nash equilibria in general-sum normal-form games
limits: this is a curator-drawn scope boundary: the text's implication (p. 116) is about Nash-equilibrium-seeking algorithms in general games, and should not be read as a hardness result for other solution objectives (e.g. common-reward optimal joint policy, which the text itself notes is solvable as an MDP via central learning, Section 5.3.1)

statement: Central Q-learning (Algorithm 4) requires observation of the full joint state and maintains Q(s,a) over the full joint-action space A=A1x...xAn; in common-reward stochastic games, using r=ri as the scalar reward together with an optimal single-agent RL algorithm guarantees the learned central policy pi_c is Pareto-optimal and, consequently, a correlated equilibrium.
conditions: common-reward stochastic games; the single-agent RL algorithm used to train pi_c must be optimal (guaranteed to find the optimal policy of the induced MDP)
limits: for zero-sum and general-sum stochastic games, the text states no known scalar reward transformation is guaranteed to yield an equilibrium policy; central learning's joint-action space grows exponentially in the number of agents (illustrated: 3 agents x 6 actions = 216 joint actions in level-based foraging)

statement: Independent Q-learning (Algorithm 5) has each agent i observe only its own local state/reward/action and maintain Qi(s,ai); from agent i's perspective, the other agents' changing policies enter the environment's apparent transition function Ti (Eq. 5.10), which is non-stationary and, because it depends on interaction history rather than just the current state, non-Markovian.
conditions: independent learning with agents using local histories only
limits: as a consequence, independent-learning approaches may produce unstable learning and may not converge to any game solution; the non-stationarity is formally distinct from single-agent bootstrapping non-stationarity

statement: Prospective link: Equation 5.10's formal definition of how other agents' changing policies enter agent i's apparent (non-Markovian) transition function Ti is a textbook-level formalization of the non-stationarity that any concurrently-trained multi-agent skill-discovery method, including HMASD-style architectures, must address when multiple agents' policies (or skill assignments) change during training.
conditions: prospective connection only; not a claim the book makes about HMASD or any specific downstream method
limits: this row is a curator-authored connection, not a source claim; no HMASD result is used as evidence for or against the book's content, and no book content is used as validated evidence for HMASD

statement: The Wunder, Littman, and Babes (2010) convergence predictions for independent Q-learning across six game subclasses (Figure 5.2, p. 128) are derived from an idealized model using infinitesimal learning steps (alpha to 0) and are stated only for general-sum normal-form games with exactly two agents and two actions each; the text does not extend these convergence predictions to larger numbers of agents, larger action spaces, or non-infinitesimal (practical) learning rates.
conditions: bounded to the cited idealized analytical model
limits: curator-drawn: a reader should not treat this game-class convergence table as evidence for IQL behavior at N>2 agents, larger action sets, or finite (non-infinitesimal) step sizes

statement: In a fixed 2-agent, 11x11-grid level-based foraging comparison (50 independent training runs, gamma=0.99, alpha=0.01, epsilon linearly decayed from 1 to 0.05 over 80,000 training steps), independent Q-learning (IQL) learns faster early in training than central Q-learning (CQL) because each IQL agent explores only 6 actions per state versus CQL's 36 (6^2) joint actions, though both algorithms eventually converge to the same optimal joint policy, solvable in 13 time steps.
conditions: single fixed 2-agent task instance with fixed start state, item levels, and grid layout; specific hyperparameters as stated
limits: this is the authors' own demonstration on one fixed task instance and one fixed agent count; not a general claim about IQL vs. CQL sample efficiency across tasks or agent counts

statement: The Section 5.3.3 level-based foraging CQL-vs-IQL comparison is run at a single fixed agent count (N=2) on a single fixed task instance; the text does not test or claim generalization of either algorithm's relative performance, convergence speed, or joint-action-space scaling behavior to a different or held-out number of agents.
conditions: bounded to the single fixed-N experiment described in the text
limits: curator-drawn: a fixed-N comparison at N=2 is not evidence for how CQL or IQL would compare at other agent counts, even though Section 5.4.4 separately discusses how joint-action-space size would grow with N in this same environment (216 to 7,776 actions from 3 to 5 agents)

statement: The authors state that the only provable convergence guarantees they cite for MARL algorithms under non-stationarity -- IGA converging to the average reward of a Nash equilibrium (Eq. 5.8), and WoLF-IGA converging to a Nash equilibrium itself (Eq. 5.3) -- are both explicitly limited to normal-form games with exactly two agents and exactly two actions.
conditions: normal-form games, n=2 agents, 2 actions per agent
limits: the authors explicitly flag this as a scope restriction, not a general MARL convergence guarantee; results are cited (IGA and WoLF-IGA algorithms detailed later in Sections 6.4.1 and 6.4.3, outside this range) rather than proved here

statement: In the Stag Hunt game, (S,S) is the Pareto-optimal, higher-reward 'reward-dominant' equilibrium requiring mutual cooperation, while (H,H) is the lower-reward but lower-risk 'risk-dominant' equilibrium (each agent can unilaterally guarantee a reward of at least 2); the authors argue algorithms such as independent Q-learning, being uncertain about other agents' actions early in training, are prone to converging to the risk-dominant equilibrium via a self-reinforcing feedback loop.
conditions: Stag Hunt matrix game structure; independent learning with exploration under uncertainty about other agents
limits: this is a qualitative argument (not a proven convergence result) about a systematic bias, illustrated with one matrix game

statement: Multi-agent credit assignment (determining whose actions among multiple agents contributed to a received reward) is distinguished from temporal credit assignment (determining which past actions contributed to a reward); the authors state multi-agent credit assignment is not specific to common-reward settings -- even with per-agent differentiated rewards, an agent must still infer whether another agent's action contributed to its own reward.
conditions: general multi-agent RL settings, illustrated with a three-agent level-based foraging example (Figure 5.7) under both common and differentiated reward variants
limits: the claim that credit assignment exists beyond common-reward settings is argued via one modified example, not a general proof

statement: Difference rewards (Wolpert and Tumer 2002; Tumer and Agogino 2007) address multi-agent credit assignment by computing a counterfactual reward with one agent's action replaced by a default ('do nothing') action, but the authors state it is generally unclear whether such a default action exists for a given environment and, if so, what it should be.
conditions: applies to environments where a meaningful default/no-op action can be defined per agent
limits: explicit authors' caveat about the generality of the default-action assumption, not a proof that difference rewards fail; contrasted with learned value-decomposition approaches (Rashid et al. 2018; Sunehag et al. 2018; Son et al. 2019; Zhou, Liu, et al. 2020), detailed later in Chapter 9 outside this range

statement: The joint-action space size grows as |A|=|A1|*...*|An| (Eq. 5.11), exemplified by level-based foraging growing from 216 joint actions at 3 agents to 7,776 at 5 agents; but this exponential growth is not inherent to having more agents -- the authors give a counter-example in which a fixed global action vector (e.g. a 1,000-variable power plant with k possible values per variable, k^1,000 total actions) is factored across n agents, keeping the total joint-action count (k^1,000) constant regardless of n, even as each individual agent's action space shrinks.
conditions: growth depends on whether each additional agent adds new decision variables (level-based foraging case) versus partitions a fixed existing action vector (power-plant case)
limits: the counter-example is illustrative/hypothetical, not an empirical result; the authors still affirm that scaling to many agents is an important open MARL research goal even when raw joint-action count does not grow

statement: The authors distinguish algorithm self-play (all agents use the same learning algorithm, the standard assumption underlying essentially all MARL algorithms presented in the book and the game-theoretic 'interactive learning' literature) from policy self-play (a single policy is trained directly against itself, as in TD-Gammon and later deep-RL self-play systems); policy self-play implies algorithm self-play and can learn faster by pooling experience into one policy, but requires symmetrical agent roles and egocentric observations, while algorithm self-play permits agents with different actions, observations, and rewards.
conditions: policy self-play requires symmetric roles and egocentric observations across agents; algorithm self-play has no such requirement
limits: distinction is the authors' own terminology introduced to disambiguate two senses of 'self-play' found in the literature

statement: Albrecht and Ramamoorthy (2012) empirically compared Nash-Q, JAL-AM, WoLF-PHC, and a regret-matching variant across many normal-form games in a mixed-play setting using multiple solution-concept-based metrics, and concluded there was no clear overall winner among the tested algorithms, each having relative strengths and limitations.
evidence_type: empirical figure reproduced from cited paper
conditions: mixed-play setting (agents use different learning algorithms), many normal-form games, non-repeated setting
limits: cited empirical study, not reproduced in this book; the comparison metrics are described only at a high level in this text

statement: Papoudakis et al. (2021), as cited in this chapter, benchmarks deep-learning-based MARL algorithms only for algorithm self-play in common-reward games; the authors explicitly state there is currently no comparable benchmark study for deep-learning-based MARL algorithms in mixed-play settings, so results from common-reward algorithm-self-play benchmarks should not be read as evidence about mixed-play or heterogeneous-algorithm behavior.
conditions: bounded to the specific gap the authors name: deep MARL algorithms, mixed-play settings
limits: curator-drawn from the authors' own explicitly stated gap; any HMASD-style comparison to deep MARL baselines evaluated only in self-play should not be extrapolated to mixed-play robustness claims

statement: Value iteration for stochastic games (Algorithm 6) converges to the unique optimal value functions V*_i because the update operator of Equation 6.4 is a gamma-contraction mapping under the max-norm, so repeated application converges to a unique fixed point by the Banach fixed-point theorem.
section: 6.1 Dynamic Programming for Games: Value Iteration
conditions: zero-sum, two-agent stochastic game; Valuei computed as the minimax value of the per-state normal-form game; discount factor gamma in [0,1)
limits: proof sketch summarized in text, full derivation attributed to Shapley (1953); established only for the two-agent zero-sum case, though the algorithm template is suggested (not proved) to generalize

statement: The value iteration algorithm for stochastic games reduces exactly to standard MDP value iteration in the single-agent special case, since the minimax Valuei operator collapses to a max-operator over a single agent's action values.
section: 6.1 Dynamic Programming for Games: Value Iteration
conditions: single-agent stochastic game (i.e., an MDP)
limits: a consistency check for the N=1 boundary case only; does not itself bear on behavior for N>2 agents

statement: Minimax Q-learning is guaranteed to learn the unique minimax value of a two-agent zero-sum stochastic game, provided all combinations of states and joint actions are tried infinitely often and the usual learning-rate conditions from single-agent RL hold.
conditions: two-agent zero-sum stochastic games; infinite visitation of all state/joint-action pairs; standard Robbins-Monro-style learning-rate schedule
limits: convergence result attributed externally to Littman and Szepesvari (1996), not proved in this text; applies only to two-agent zero-sum games

statement: In a simplified two-agent zero-sum soccer game, a policy learned by minimax Q-learning won 53.7% of episodes against a hand-built opponent (close to the theoretical 50%) and 37.5% against an optimal worst-case opponent, while independent Q-learning won 76.3% against the hand-built opponent (by exploiting its weaknesses) but 0% against the optimal opponent.
evidence_type: empirical figure reproduced from cited paper
conditions: 4x5 grid-world soccer game, two agents, one million training time steps, exploration rate epsilon=0.2, initial learning rate alpha=1.0 decayed by factor 0.9999954 per step, discount gamma=0.9, tested over 100,000 time steps per opponent type; results reproduced from Littman (1994)
limits: single task/environment (grid-world soccer); results are from the original 1994 paper, not an independent replication by these authors

statement: Nash Q-learning converges to a Nash equilibrium of a general-sum stochastic game only if, in addition to infinite exploration of state/joint-action pairs and standard learning-rate conditions, every normal-form game encountered during learning consistently has either (a) a global optimum for all agents or (b) a saddle point.
conditions: general-sum stochastic games, any finite number of agents; every per-state normal-form game Gamma_s must have a global optimum in all encountered games, or a saddle point in all encountered games (not merely some)
limits: the authors state this condition is 'highly restrictive' and unlikely to hold in any encountered game, let alone all of them

statement: The book's Nash Q-learning convergence guarantee is conditioned on every per-state game encountered during learning satisfying the global-optimum-or-saddle-point structural property; this restrictive-condition guarantee is not evidence that Nash Q-learning converges in general N-agent stochastic games lacking that property.

statement: GIGA achieves no-regret: with step size kappa_k = 1/sqrt(k), the regret of an agent using GIGA is bounded by Regret^k_i <= [sqrt(k) + (sqrt(k)-1)/2] * |Ai| * r_max^2, so the average regret goes to zero as k approaches infinity, and this no-regret property implies the empirical action distribution converges to a coarse correlated equilibrium; the result also implies IGA achieves no-regret, and extends to games with more than two agents by replacing the single opponent with the joint action of all other agents.

statement: Deep Q-learning replaces the tabular Q-learning update with a neural network Q(s,a;θ) trained by minimizing the squared error between Q(s_t,a_t;θ) and a bootstrapped target y_t, where y_t = r_t if s_{t+1} is terminal and y_t = r_t + γ max_{a'} Q(s_{t+1},a';θ) otherwise (Equations 8.2–8.3, Algorithm 10).

statement: The book defines the 'deadly triad' (citing Sutton and Barto 2018; van Hasselt et al. 2018) as the combination of off-policy learning, function approximation, and bootstrapped targets, and states this combination 'can lead to unstable and diverging value estimates.'
conditions: Applies to algorithms combining all three components simultaneously, e.g., deep Q-learning with off-policy (ε-greedy) experience.
limits: The book states divergence, as it explains the mechanism, requires all three components together: removing function approximation, bootstrapping, or off-policy sampling individually prevents the described divergence mechanism (p. 217–218).

statement: The book states that RL violates both parts of the i.i.d. assumption underlying most machine learning: consecutive experience samples are correlated because s_{t+1} and r_t are determined by the transition function conditioned on s_t and a_t, and the sampling distribution shifts as the policy changes; a replay buffer D storing past transitions, from which mini-batches are sampled uniformly at random (B ~ U(D)), is introduced to break these correlations (Algorithm 12 / DQN).
conditions: The replay buffer is implemented as a fixed-capacity FIFO queue; it can only be used for off-policy algorithms because stored experiences were generated by earlier versions of the behavior policy.
limits: The text explicitly states a replay buffer 'cannot be used to update a policy following the policy gradient theorem' (p. 227) since on-policy algorithms require data generated by the current policy.

statement: In a single-agent 8x8 level-based-foraging item-collection task, an ablation compares deep Q-learning, deep Q-learning + target network, deep Q-learning + replay buffer, and full DQN (target network + replay buffer) over 100,000 time steps, five seeds; only the full DQN combination yields 'a stable and quick increase in performance and convergence to near-optimal discounted returns' (Figure 8.3), while target networks alone give 'no notable improvement' and a replay buffer alone remains 'noisy across runs.'

statement: DQN is stated to be 'prone to overestimation of action values' because the target uses max_{a'} Q(s_{t+1},a';θ); double deep Q-networks (DDQN) reduces this by decoupling greedy action selection (via the main network's arg max) from action-value evaluation (via the target network), per Equation 8.6.

statement: The book states that combining DDQN, prioritized experience replay (Schaul et al. 2016), parameterized exploration noise (Fortunato et al. 2018), dueling value/advantage decomposition (Wang et al. 2016), and distributional value learning (Bellemare, Dabney, and Munos 2017) yields the Rainbow algorithm, 'shown to exhibit significantly higher performance than DQN across Atari games (Hessel et al. 2018).'
conditions: Comparison reported by Hessel et al. 2018 on the Atari benchmark, cited secondhand by this textbook.

statement: The policy gradient theorem's expectation is defined under the state distribution Pr(s|π) and action distribution π(·|s;ϕ) of the current policy π being optimized; the book states this 'clearly illustrates the restriction that follows from the policy gradient theorem: the optimization of the parameterized policy is limited to on-policy data' and that data from any different policy π′ — including older versions of π obtained earlier in training — 'can not be used to update π following the policy gradient theorem.'
conditions: Policy gradient theorem (Sutton and Barto 2018) as stated by the authors; applies to episodic environments; requires a differentiable policy parameterization.
limits: Q^π(s,a) in the theorem must itself be approximated since it is not known a priori; the book notes DQN-style algorithms do not satisfy the on-policy requirement because they approximate the optimal value function via the Bellman optimality equation instead.

statement: REINFORCE (Williams 1992) instantiates the policy gradient theorem with Monte Carlo estimates of episodic returns, minimizing L(ϕ) = -(1/T) Σ_t (Σ_{τ≥t} γ^{τ-t} r_τ) log π(a_t|s_t;ϕ) (Equations 8.15–8.16, Algorithm 13); the book states 'Monte Carlo return estimates have high variance, which leads to high variance of gradients and unstable training in REINFORCE' because returns depend on the entire episode's states and actions.
conditions: Requires full episode rollouts (updates occur after episode termination); on-policy Monte Carlo returns.
limits: High-variance gradients are stated as an explicit limitation of the base algorithm without a baseline.

statement: The book derives (Equations 8.17–8.27) that subtracting any baseline b(s), defined only over the state s, from Q^π(s,a) in the policy gradient theorem leaves the expected gradient unchanged, because Σ_a b(s)∇_ϕπ(a|s;ϕ) = b(s)∇_ϕ Σ_a π(a|s;ϕ) = b(s)∇_ϕ 1 = 0; a state-value function V(s;θ), trained by minimizing L(θ)=(1/T)Σ_t(u_t - V(s_t;θ))², is given as a common baseline choice.
conditions: The baseline must be a function of state only (not of the action) for the derivation to hold.
limits: none

statement: Actor-critic algorithms use a critic V to compute bootstrapped return estimates (Equations 8.30–8.32) instead of full Monte Carlo returns; the book states this gives two benefits — updates from a single time step's experience rather than waiting for episode end, and lower variance than Monte Carlo returns — 'at a price of introduced bias, because the used value function might not (yet) approximate the true expected returns of states.'
conditions: Requires a trained critic V(s;θ); the bootstrapped estimate uses one-step (or N-step) lookahead.
limits: Bias is explicitly acknowledged as the cost of bootstrapping; the book states 'we find that the trade-off of bias for lower variance often improves training stability' without a formal bound.

statement: Using a critic trained with A2C (N=5) in the single-agent level-based-foraging task, the book reports that measured variance of N-step return estimates increases with N (approaching Monte Carlo variance at N=T) while measured bias decreases with N (approaching zero, the unbiased Monte Carlo case), shown for N∈{1,...,10} plus Monte Carlo in Figure 8.5.
conditions: Measured post hoc from 10,000 evaluation episodes collected with a policy trained for 100,000 time steps with N=5 in one specific environment.
limits: Single environment, single trained policy; the book presents this to illustrate the general bias-variance trade-off qualitatively, not as a quantitative law for other tasks.

statement: Advantage actor-critic (A2C) estimates the advantage Adv(s,a) = Q(s,a) - V(s), approximated using the critic as Adv(s_t,a_t) = r_t - V(s_t;θ) if s_{t+1} terminal else r_t + γV(s_{t+1};θ) - V(s_t;θ) (Equation 8.36), and minimizes the actor loss L(ϕ) = -Adv(s_t,a_t) log π(a_t|s_t;ϕ) (Equation 8.38) jointly with a critic squared-error loss (Equation 8.40); the book denotes its presented pseudocode 'Simplified A2C' since the original A2C/A3C (Mnih et al. 2016) also uses multi-step returns and entropy regularization.
conditions: Requires both actor π(·;ϕ) and critic V(·;θ) networks trained jointly (Algorithm 14).
limits: The book explicitly flags its Algorithm 14 as a simplification of the original A2C/A3C algorithm.

statement: Entropy regularization adds the negative policy entropy, -H(π(·|s;ϕ)) = Σ_a π(a|s;ϕ) log π(a|s;ϕ) (Equation 8.41), to the actor loss; the book states that maximizing entropy 'penalizes the policy for assigning a very high probability to any action' and 'discourages premature convergence to a suboptimal close-to-deterministic policy,' thereby incentivizing exploration.
conditions: Applied as an additional term added to the actor loss; the original A2C/A3C uses it, while the book's 'Simplified A2C' (Algorithm 14) omits it by default.
limits: none

statement: The book contrasts trust region policy optimization (TRPO, Schulman et al. 2015), which 'constrains each optimization step... to a small trust region' but 'requires either solving a constrained optimization problem or computing a penalty term, which are both computationally expensive,' with PPO's clipped surrogate objective, described as computationally efficient.
conditions: The comparison is qualitative/conceptual, not a reported head-to-head experiment in this chapter.
limits: No empirical comparison of TRPO vs. PPO is presented in this section; the comparison is descriptive.

statement: PPO (Schulman et al. 2017, clipped-objective variant) computes an importance sampling ratio ρ(s,a) = π(a|s;ϕ)/π_β(a|s) (Equation 8.42) between the policy being optimized and the behavior policy that generated the data, and minimizes L(ϕ) = -min(ρ(s_t,a_t)·Adv(s_t,a_t), clip(ρ(s_t,a_t), 1-ε, 1+ε)·Adv(s_t,a_t)) (Equation 8.43, Algorithm 15); this clipping lets PPO reuse the same batch of data for N_e update epochs, unlike standard on-policy policy gradient methods that require freshly on-policy data for every update.
conditions: ε is a hyperparameter bounding how far the updated policy's action probability may diverge from π_β; requires a critic for the advantage estimate (Equation 8.36).
limits: The book describes only the clipped-surrogate PPO variant in detail, noting Schulman et al. (2017) also propose a KL-divergence-penalty variant that it does not detail.

statement: In the single-agent level-based-foraging task (Figure 8.3(a)), REINFORCE, A2C (N=5), and PPO (N=5, ε=0.2, N_e=4 epochs) are trained for 100,000 time steps across five seeds (Figure 8.6): REINFORCE 'learns to solve the task in most runs' but with 'high variance... all throughout training'; A2C and PPO with N-step returns 'reach the optimal performance across all runs within 60,000 time steps'; PPO 'is able to learn slightly faster than A2C, which can be explained by its optimization being able to use each batch of experiences multiple times.'
conditions: Small actor/critic networks (two layers, 32 hidden units), γ=0.99; REINFORCE learning rate 1e-3 without baseline; A2C/PPO learning rate 3e-4, N=5.
limits: Single fixed small-scale single-agent task; not a general ranking claim across environments.

statement: Because 'on-policy policy gradient algorithms cannot make use of a replay buffer,' the book presents synchronous data collection (parallel environment instances, agent waits for all threads each step, Algorithm 16/Figure 8.7) and asynchronous training (each thread holds its own agent copy and environment, updates a shared central network, Figure 8.9) as the two techniques used instead to break correlations and obtain larger batches for on-policy algorithms.

statement: In a 12x12 level-based-foraging task requiring collection of two items, simplified A2C is trained for five minutes with K ∈ {1,4,16,64} synchronous environments (Figure 8.8): smaller K is comparably sample-efficient per time step but less stable (K=1 'does not converge to the optimal policy'), while larger K is more wall-clock efficient, though 'these benefits diminish with a growing number of synchronous environments' due to threads idling while waiting for the slowest thread.

statement: For partially observable environments, the book states that value functions and policies 'should be conditioned on the episodic history of observations, h_t = (o_0,...,o_t)'; rather than concatenating or zero-padding the growing history (called impractical, and for zero-padding 'not applicable to tasks with potentially infinite episodes'), it recommends using a recurrent neural network to process the history one observation at a time, with GRUs and LSTMs cited as the RNN architectures 'commonly used in deep RL.'

statement: In independent learning, each agent treats the other agents as part of a non-stationary component of the environment rather than modeling them explicitly; as other agents' policies change, the transition, observation, and reward functions perceived by each individual agent change too, which the authors state can lead to unstable learning and poor convergence, despite independent learning often performing well in practice.
conditions: applies to fully decentralized training and execution where agents cannot or do not model other agents
limits: the authors note this is a known challenge, not a proof of failure in all cases; independent learning 'often performs well in practice'

statement: Centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) is defined as training that may use centrally shared information (e.g. all agents' observation histories or the full state) to update agent policies, while each agent's deployed policy is conditioned only on its own local observation history, so it can be executed independently; the value function used during training is no longer needed at execution time.
conditions: applies when the application scenario allows privileged information to be shared only during training, not at deployment
limits: none stated in this passage

statement: Off-policy independent learning with a replay buffer (e.g. IDQN) can retain stale experience: as illustrated by a chess example where agent 2 learns to counter agent 1's opening, agent 1's replay buffer continues to hold now-outdated transitions that overstate the old opening's value, which can delay agent 1 from abandoning the countered strategy.
conditions: applies to off-policy algorithms using a replay buffer under concurrent multi-agent learning
limits: illustrative example, not an empirical measurement; mitigations discussed include smaller buffers, importance-sampling reweighting (Foerster et al. 2017), hysteretic Q-learning, and leniency

statement: IDQN (Algorithm 17) gives each agent i its own action-value network Q(.;theta_i), its own target network, and its own replay buffer D_i; each agent's DQN loss (Eq. 9.1) is computed only from that agent's own local observation history, action, and reward, with no information sharing between agents at training or execution time, though all agents' losses are optimized simultaneously.
conditions: fully decentralized training and execution
limits: none stated beyond the general independent-learning caveats

statement: On-policy independent algorithms such as REINFORCE are stated to be less susceptible to the replay-buffer staleness problem than off-policy algorithms like IDQN, because they always learn from experience generated under the most recent (current) policies of the other agents.
conditions: applies to on-policy independent policy-gradient methods (REINFORCE, A2C, PPO) versus off-policy value-based methods with replay buffers
limits: stated as a qualitative advantage, not quantified

statement: Under CTDE, the actor network is conditioned only on agent i's local observation history h_i^t to preserve decentralized execution, while the critic (discarded after training) may be conditioned on any additional information beyond the agent's own history and action, including other agents' observation histories or the full environment state, forming a vector z; the critic's value loss (Eq. 9.10) uses this z as part of its input.

statement: Difference rewards (Eq. 9.14) approximate agent i's contribution to a common reward as the difference between the actual received reward and the reward agent i would have received under a chosen default action, holding other agents' actions fixed; the aristocrat utility (Eq. 9.15) avoids needing a default action by instead subtracting the expected reward agent i would receive under its current policy.

conditions: Restricted to two-agent, two-action, strictly ordinal (no tied outcome ranks) normal-form games.
limits: The taxonomy only covers 2x2 strictly ordinal games; it is not claimed to generalize to larger action/agent counts or games with tied or cardinal payoffs.

statement: In level-based foraging (LBF), n agents act in a fully observable grid-world with a discrete action space {up, down, left, right, collect, noop}; a group of adjacent agents can jointly collect an item only if they all select collect and the sum of their skill levels meets or exceeds the item's level, so higher-level items require cooperation among a subset of agents while lower-level items can be collected individually. Each task fixes the number of agents as a configuration parameter.
conditions: Grid size, number of agents/items, and skill-level assignment are all task parameters; levels can be randomized per episode.
limits: The equation defining the per-agent reward (Eq. 11.1, p. 354) falls in a chunk (B01-C0077) flagged equation_text_unreliable, so its extracted summation symbols should not be trusted; consult the source page for the exact formula.

statement: LBF's 'forced cooperation' task variant assigns item levels such that every item in the environment requires all agents in the task to cooperate to collect it, in contrast to the default random-level variant where some items are individually collectible and agents may compete for them.
conditions: A specific configuration of the LBF task family, not the default; illustrated for an 8x8 grid, 3 agents, 5 items in Figure 11.2(b).
limits: This is one specific LBF task configuration among many possible parameterizations; the book states LBF is flexible across degrees of cooperation, observability, and scale.

statement: The multi-agent particle environment (MPE) contains 2D navigation tasks spanning competitive, cooperative, and common-reward objectives with both full and partial observability, and both discrete cardinal-direction and continuous velocity action options; named tasks include predator-prey, coordinated navigation (3 agents, 3 landmarks), and speaker-listener, the last of which requires a speaker agent to communicate a hidden landmark color to a listener agent via binary communication actions.
conditions: Task-dependent: observability, reward structure (competitive/cooperative/common-reward), and action type (discrete/continuous) vary by which MPE task is configured.
limits: none

statement: In SMAC, all tasks are partially observable (agents see health/shield status of themselves and nearby units within a radius), the team is rewarded with a dense common reward for damage dealt/units defeated plus a win bonus, and it plays against a fixed built-in AI. The authors state the shared common reward makes credit assignment especially prominent because actions (e.g., destroying a unit early) have long-term consequences that are hard to disentangle under one shared signal, which the authors say makes value-decomposition methods particularly suitable for SMAC.
conditions: Team size and unit composition are fixed per task/map; SMAC always pits the learned team against a fixed built-in AI opponent, not another learned team.
limits: none

statement: Each SMAC task fixes the starting locations of all units, which the authors state can cause agents to overfit to that specific configuration (e.g., learning to act in a fixed order irrespective of state) rather than learning generalizable policies; SMACv2 (Ellis et al. 2023, cited) was proposed to randomize unit types and starting locations across episodes to address this. SMAClite (Michalski, Christianos, and Albrecht 2023, cited) reimplements SMAC without the StarCraft II game, and the authors report SMAClite-trained agents transfer to SMAC with some performance degradation, i.e., SMAC is accurately but not perfectly modeled by SMAClite.
conditions: The overfitting concern and SMACv2/SMAClite findings are attributed to the cited external papers, not independently reproduced in this book.
limits: The transfer-degradation finding is reported secondhand from the cited SMAClite paper; the book does not restate the magnitude of degradation. Fixed-per-task starting locations should not be read as evidence that SMAC agents generalize across configurations.

statement: In RWARE, agents receive individual (not shared) positive rewards only upon successfully delivering a requested shelf, making rewards very sparse since delivery requires long, specific action sequences; the authors state this sparsity makes parameter and experience sharing (Section 9.7) particularly well suited to RWARE, as demonstrated by Christianos, Schäfer, and Albrecht (2020, cited).
conditions: Applies to RWARE's default individual-reward, sparse-delivery-reward structure; observation range (partial observability) and warehouse layout/agent count are task parameters.
limits: The parameter/experience-sharing benefit is attributed to the cited 2020 paper's demonstration, not re-derived in this chapter.

statement: Google Research Football (GRF) supports a multi-agent interface with either two agents (one controlling each whole team) or per-player agent control of a cooperating team (up to full 11 vs. 11) against a fixed built-in AI, offers two selectable reward functions (goal-only, or additionally shaped for possession/forward progress) and three observation modes (pixel, compressed global map, or a 115-value feature vector).
conditions: Reward function and observation mode are both independently selectable settings of the environment; agent count depends on whether whole-team or per-player control is chosen.
limits: none

statement: Hanabi is a fully cooperative, turn-based card game for two to five players in which each player sees every other player's cards but not their own, and communication is restricted to a shared pool of eight information tokens spent on hints; the authors state (citing Bard et al. 2020) that agents must adopt implicit conventions beyond the literal hint content to succeed, making Hanabi relevant to cooperative self-play, ad hoc teamwork, and acting under imperfect information.
conditions: Player count is fixed per game instance at a value between two and five, chosen before play begins; it does not vary within a game.
limits: none

statement: Two Overcooked-style implementations are described: Cooking Zoo (Rother, Weisswange, and Peters 2023), which supports customizable agent count, layouts, recipes, rewards, and observation spaces and is described as well suited to studying generalization to new tasks; and Carroll et al.'s (2019) Overcooked, similar in observation/action space but limited to a small fixed set of recipes and five map layouts with less customization, whose distinguishing advantage is a publicly available human-gameplay dataset.
conditions: Cooking Zoo's task diversity depends on its parameterization; Carroll et al.'s environment is explicitly scoped as more limited in recipes/layouts.
limits: none

statement: Melting Pot (Leibo et al. 2021) is explicitly designed to test two distinct kinds of generalization: across tasks (via a diverse set of over 50 tasks differing in agent count, objectives, and dynamics) and across co-players (via a focal population trained on one task that, during evaluation, is paired with varying background agents sampled from pretrained policies), so that evaluation measures zero-shot generalization to unfamiliar co-player behavior rather than to a different task.
conditions: The co-player generalization protocol holds the task fixed and varies only the identity/behavior of background agents drawn from a pretrained population; task-generalization is a separate, distinct axis in the same collection.
limits: This is generalization to varying co-player identity within a fixed task and agent-count setting, not evidence about generalizing a single trained policy across different agent counts (variable N) within one task.

statement: OpenSpiel (Lanctot et al. 2019) is described as focused on turn-based ('extensive-form') games, including classical games such as Backgammon, Bridge, Chess, Go, and Poker, while also supporting simultaneous-move games matching this book's own game models; environments mix full and partial observability but all specify discrete actions, observations, and states.
conditions: OpenSpiel's simultaneous-move support is stated as an additional capability beyond its primary turn-based focus.
limits: All OpenSpiel environments listed are discrete in action/observation/state; the book does not claim continuous-action coverage for OpenSpiel.

statement: Petting Zoo (Terry et al. 2021) unifies a large, heterogeneous set of multi-agent environments (Atari Learning Environment-based games, classic games such as Connect Four/Go/Texas Hold'em, continuous control tasks, and an MPE integration) behind one common interface spanning full and partial observability, discrete and continuous actions, and dense and sparse rewards.
conditions: Coverage spans multiple observability, action-type, and reward-density regimes because Petting Zoo aggregates many distinct underlying environments rather than being one environment with fixed properties.
limits: none

statement: Appendix A's survey bibliography is stated by the authors to be non-exhaustive: they explicitly note that additional survey articles about particular MARL application domains exist but were omitted from the list, which runs in reverse chronological order from Sen and Weiss (1999) (described as the first MARL survey the authors are aware of) to Zhu, Dastani, and Wang (2024).
section: A Surveys on Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
conditions: The list covers general MARL survey articles only; application-domain-specific surveys are explicitly excluded by the authors' own statement.
limits: This bibliography should not be treated as a complete inventory of all MARL surveys, only of general (non-application-specific) ones known to the authors at time of writing.
